column2: A brahmin named Dirghatapas always lived there; he practised austerity exceedingly, and so he is known as Dirghatapas.
He lived there with his wife and with his sons; all five sons stayed near him and served him.
His youngest son was Rishyashringa of great austerity, devoted to Vedic study, a celibate endowed with virtues,
ever devoted to the practice of yoga, living on bulbs, roots and fruits; he lived in the form of a deer, always dwelling among the deer.
At the beginning and end of each day the devoted son of the sage stood before his mother and father and saluted them.
Then he went back to the forest and the mountain caves, playing with the young deer; he died by a king's arrow.
The king said: "Living there in the hermitage of the great ascetic Dirghatapas, how did his youngest son come under the sway of death?"
The Blessed Lord said: Listen with one mind, lord of the earth, to a wonderful story, by merely hearing which one is freed from all sins.
The king of Kashi, a great king of great strength and valour, renowned as Chitrasena, lived in Varanasi.
Living thus in his kingdom, he said to his ministers: "I shall go hunting; you remain in charge of the kingdom."
Told "Go" by his ministers, the lord of the earth went.
Umbrella upon umbrella was seen as he went toward the forest; a great deal of dust rose there, struck up by the feet of elephants and horses,
and by it the whole circle of the earth with the sun was covered; neither the sun nor the quarters nor the moon could be seen there,
nor the trees nor the mountain slopes anywhere. There, great king, a herd of deer was seen.
All the men ran, with the king and the princes; their company broke up and they quickly went off in the ten directions.
King Chitrasena, lord of the earth, went along one path; he went alone wherever those deer went.
Then he entered a difficult forest empty of birds, thick with anthills, bushes and creepers, and once he had entered it he could no longer be seen.
He saw himself alone, with neither horse nor foot soldiers: "No one knows where I am here, and I do not know the ten directions."
Thus King Chitrasena, lord of men, fell into distress; he took refuge in the shade there and rested again and again.
Wandering tormented by hunger and thirst in the difficult forest and the mountain caves, he then saw a divine lake adorned with clusters of lotuses,
crowded with swans and karandava ducks and resounding with chakravaka birds. Seeing the lake, the king of kings was thrilled with joy;
gathering white lotuses, he bathed there, and satisfied the ancestors, gods and men according to rule,
and drank the clear water as much as he wished. Coming out of the water onto the bank, he saw a tree nearby
and sat down in thought: "What am I to do?" Then he saw many deer taking shelter in the shade in a part of the forest,
some facing east, others facing south, some facing the west and some turned toward the north;
some were sleeping, others stood with ears pricked up. Among the deer stood the yogi Rishyashringa of great austerity.
Seeing the deer, the king thought of striking: "I shall kill a deer and eat as I please;
by eating deer's flesh I shall recover, and then I shall go to Kashi, searching for the road."
Having reflected thus, the king took his stand at the foot of the tree, grasped his bow with his hand and let fly the arrow.
As soon as the arrow was shot, all the deer vanished; but among them the one, Rishyashringa of great austerity,
pierced by the arrow, fell and cried "Krishna, Krishna!" He cried out, "Alas, by whom have I been struck down now?
Whose evil thought is this, that his mind turned against me? I was standing among the deer and did no wrong."
Hearing that human voice, the king was filled with wonder; going quickly, he saw a brahmin shining with brahmin splendour.
Alas, alas, what a grievous thing I have done today, that I have killed him! The brahmin said: "You will have no success at all when I have died.
The killing will be laid on you alone when I have died. My mother and father are old, and my brothers are ascetics;
my brothers' wives will die when I have died. These killings will be yours — how can you be purified?
I shall tell you a remedy, if you are willing to carry it out."
The king said: "Tell me today the remedy that is in your mind; I will do it all with effort, great sage."
Shringi said: "I ask you: where are you from, who are you, and how did you come here? Among brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas — or are you a shudra or an outcaste?"
The king said: "I am not a brahmin, nor a vaishya, nor a shudra; I am a kshatriya." Shringi said: "Take me to the holy hermitage where my parents are,
and announce yourself as one who has come bearing the sin against their son; seeing me, the two will have compassion on you,
or they will devise a remedy by which there will be peace." Hearing his words, Chitrasena, best of kings,
placed the brahmin on his shoulder and set out for the hermitage; he could not carry him and rested again and again.
Then he saw the brahmin fainting, his senses failing; Chitrasena set him down in the shade of a banyan tree,
and having rested, speaking to him again and again — while he watched, king of kings, Rishyashringa of great austerity,
knower of yoga, quickly passed away through the yoga of meditation. He cremated the brahmin with the rite laid down by rule,
bathed, and, afflicted with grief, wept and fainted. Then the king fell into the greatest anxiety:

How shall I go home to Varanasi now? I am ruined. Seized by the killing of a brahmin, I shall offer my body into the fire.
skandapuran:89:57	Or, following the sage's word, I shall go to the hermitage and tell the great sage what happened.
Reflecting thus, the king went near the hermitage; taking up Rishyashringa's bones, the best of kings
stood in the line of sight of the brahmin sage of cultivated self. Dirghatapas said: "Come, you are welcome today; sit on this seat.
I am Dirghatapas; here for you today is the madhuparka with a seat of grass." The king said: "I am not worthy even of the guest-water of the great sage of cultivated self.
Your son, brahmin, standing among the deer, was killed by me; punish me, the slayer of your son, brahmin, and chastise me with a severe penalty.
Rishyashringa of great austerity was killed, brahmin, when I mistook him for a deer; knowing this, brahmin, do with me as is fitting."
Hearing his words, the mother came out of the house distraught, cried "Alas, I am slain!" and fell to the ground.
Afflicted with grief for her son, she lamented in great sorrow, crying "O son, son!" piteously like an osprey:

You were perfect in the study of the Veda, devoted to japa and oblation; when shall I ask after you again, son, when you come to the door of the house?
skandapuran:89:66	In the three worlds sandal is said to be cool, but a son's embrace is cooler even than sandal.
skandapuran:89:67	I wish to embrace you, my dearest son; bereft of you and in great sorrow I shall die.
Lamenting thus, wretched and afflicted with grief for her son, fainting, distraught and wretched, she fell to the ground.
Seeing his wife fallen, afflicted with grief for his son, the best of sages grew angry with King Chitrasena.
Dirghatapas said: "Go, go, great sinner, do not show me your face! Why, brahmin... why was my son killed by you, even unintentionally?
Many killings of brahmins will be yours, lord of men; you have come as death itself to me and my family."
Having said this, the brahmin reflected again and again, gave up his anger and then followed the way of the sages.
The sage said: "Give up your anxiety, O king; I spoke harsh words, overcome by grief for my son and fallen into sorrow, giver of honour.
What can a wise man do, driven by his own deeds? For the understanding of men generally follows their karma.
What was written for me by you has come about in just this way; but many killings of brahmins will be yours, no doubt.
Among brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas, or a shudra, or among outcastes and the like — who are you? Tell me the truth, and why was my son slain?"
Chitrasena said: "I make my plea, brahmin sage, and you must forgive me; I am not a brahmin, dear sir, nor a shudra, nor born a vaishya,
nor of outcaste birth; I am a kshatriya, best of the twice-born, the king of Kashi, who came to this excellent forest to hunt deer.
As I wandered, the sage bearing the form of a deer was struck down there. What should I do, brahmin? Tell me a remedy."
Dirghatapas said: "The killing of a brahmin cannot be crossed by one person alone, lord; it depends on place, time and one's ability — hear it, lord of men.
My four sons, O king, with their wives and their mother, will not live, nor I, because of Rishyashringa.
I shall tell you a good remedy, dear one; listen. If it can be done, lord of men, it is an easy remedy:
cremate all of us with our family in the fire, O king, and cast the bones into the water of the Narmada at Shulabheda.
On the southern bank of the Narmada is the renowned Shulabheda, a holy place that removes all sin, the very best of all holy places.
Becoming pure, cast my bones in at Shulabheda; you will be freed from all sins by my word, no doubt."
The king said: "Give the command, dear one, and I will do it, no doubt. Everything I have — kingdom, treasury, women and sons —
I give to you as a gift, brahmin; be gracious to me." While the sage and the king were thus speaking with each other, O king,
the sage's wife's heart suddenly burst and she died; overwhelmed by grief for her son, she fell lifeless on the ground.
And the sons all died from grief for their mother, and all the daughters-in-law died together with their husbands.
Seeing all those chief sages dead, he summoned the brahmins who lived in the hermitage there
and told them, best of men, what had happened; permitted by them all together, he somehow carefully cremated them.
Having purified his own body and carefully gathered the bones, the king, lord of the earth, set out southward on foot.
When he could not go on he stayed in the shade; resting and going on again, resting again and again,
carrying the bones, he bathed with his clothes on at every step; without water or food he went on facing south.
In a short time he reached the bank of the Narmada; the best of kings asked all the brahmins living in the hermitages:
Tell me, best of brahmins, the way to Shulabheda.
The brahmins said: "Go to the southern bank of the Narmada and you will see it, not otherwise."
At the sages' word the king, lord of men, went there; then he saw the holy place crowded with many brahmins,
thick with many trees and creepers, beautified with many flowers, rich with many roots and fruits, adorned with many wild beasts,
crowded with hosts of sages keeping many auspicious vows: some standing on one foot, others bright as the sun,
some standing with a fixed gaze, others with upraised arms; some devoted to the chandrayana, some fasting for a fortnight,
some fasting for a month, some fasting for a season; some eating withered leaves, some living on air,
some devoted to the practice of yoga, meditating on the supreme state; some established in household life, some keeping the agnihotra.
Seeing brahmins of this kind, he went down on his knees on the ground, bowed his head and the king spoke, O king:
In what place is that holy place? Tell me, best of the twice-born, which grants all the perfection they desire and the fruit they wish.
A sage said: "Go a hundred bow-lengths to the summit of Bhrigutunga; you will see a broad, lovely pool full of water."
Hearing their words he went to the head of the pool; on seeing that holy place the king was bewildered.
Seeing the most blessed pool, and the Ganga especially, and seeing the eastward-flowing Sarasvati, the king was bewildered.
Then, filled with wonder and pondering again and again, he saw an osprey in the sky carrying flesh,
circling, set upon and attacked by birds without flesh; all the flesh-eaters fought with one another.
Struck by blows of beaks, the osprey fell into the water where long ago the trident-bearer split the ground with his trident;
by the power of that holy place it at once became a man. Seeing the curlew in an aerial car bearing a divine form,
sung to by apsarases, the king came to that holy place; setting the bones on the ground and bathing according to rule,
he satisfied his chosen deities with water mixed with sesame; then the king took the bones and cast them into the water.
Then, after gazing for a moment, the king stood looking upward and saw them all, bearing the lovely forms of gods,
clad in divine garments and adorned with divine ornaments, in divine golden aerial cars attended by hosts of apsarases.
Seeing them all, each separately established in an aerial car, flying up, the king was delighted.
The sage, mounted in his aerial car, then said to Chitrasena: "Well done, well done, great king Chitrasena of great mind!
By your grace, best of kings, a divine goal is mine today; this that you have done is supremely difficult;
even one's own son cannot do such a thing for the ancestors. By my word, O king, you will become free of sin,
and you will see what you desire, king of kings, whatever your mind wishes." Then, having given his blessing to the wise Chitrasena,
the sage Dirghatapas went to heaven with his sons.
We shall go to the head of the pool, and the three gods then stood there and said thus to one another: "This holy place is likewise auspicious.
As Gayashira is holy and is recited in every month, so Shulabheda on the bank of the Reva is holy, no doubt."
Brahma said: "This holy place, great king, is as holy as Gayashira; a man who bathes in that water becomes spotless.
Apart from Gayashira alone, Shankara, all the holy places are not worth a sixteenth part of the holy place Shulabheda.
To the south of the pool its measure is ten cubits; to the east, west and north-west the measure is twenty-one.
This is the extent of the holy place for pinda offerings and other rites; all those who have given gifts here are holy men.
Vishnu, in the form of the three-eyed one, and the Grandsire in the form of Brahma dwell ever at that holy place and accept worship given with devotion.
The forefathers watch each son as he is born: 'When will this son go there? When will he become a giver?'
The devoted man who performs shraddha at the five places rescues all his family members who have become pretas —
twenty-one of the father's side, twenty-one of the mother's side and eleven of the wife's; he rescues all of these.
By the grace of the twice-born, the gods and the ancestors, the giver of shraddha dwells where the god Maheshvara is.
Those who have killed themselves, killers of cows, those slain by women, those killed by tusked beasts, by falling into water or by lightning —
for them there is no cremation, no purification and no water rite; but whoever performs shraddha for them at that holy place with devotion,
they attain release at the three places, no doubt, and their satisfaction lasts a year, no doubt.
Sin done unknowingly, sin done in childhood — all of it perishes quickly by a single bath, lord of the earth.
As a cloth washed by a washerman becomes spotless, so one smeared with sin who bathes at this holy place becomes spotless.
Whoever takes renunciation at that holy place, lord of men, meditating on Mahadeva, goes to the supreme state;
having sported as he wishes, at his own will, in Shiva's abode, he is born in a great family, knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedangas,
handsome and fortunate, free from all diseases, endowed with every dharma and possessed of all good conduct.
This I have told you, O king, the excellent fruit of the holy place; a man who hears it constantly is freed from all sins.
Whoever with devotion causes this story to be heard in the presence of brahmins, and recites it at shraddha, in a temple and at every festival,
with him the gods are pleased, and men with the ancestors; for those who recite and hear it the mass of sin perishes.
Whoever writes out the greatness of the holy place and gives it to brahmins obtains remembrance of former births and gains the fruit he desires."
The holy one named Devashila — its excellent greatness, tell me all of this by your grace, Supreme Person.
Rudra said: Listen with one mind to how the Ganga was brought down. Long ago, fortunate one, the goddess — Brahma and all the gods
petitioned the lord of the world, god of gods, guru of the world; the Ganga, who had been held in a pot, was released onto the fair earth,
and then the Bharati was released by Rudra from his head onto the earth. Men who bathe with devotion at the holy place on her bank
and ever drink her water do not go to Yama's abode — where she fell into the pool at Shulabheda, lord of men.
To the west of the divine river, where the eastward-flowing Sarasvati is, and to the south, is the unsurpassed holy place called Shulabheda.
There is the lovely Devashila, made by the god himself. Whoever bathes there and feeds a brahmin with devotion, O king,
even for a small gift there is no end to its merit. Uttanapada said: "Which gifts are praised on earth, lord of the gods,
by giving which with devotion a man is freed from all sins? The greatness of Devashila, the fruit from bathing and giving,
and what is to be gained by vows, fasts and restraints — tell me that." The Blessed Lord said: "Long ago there was a lord of the Chedis, of great valour and great strength,
renowned as Virasena, overlord of the rulers of provinces; in his kingdom there was no enemy, no disease and no thief,
nor was there adharma there, only dharma always. The king was ever joyful, with his wife and many sons.
He had one daughter, lovely like Girija; she was cherished by her father and mother together with all their kin.
When the time came, the marriage rite was performed according to rule; then, in the twelfth year, the lord of the Chedis, the great lord —
then her husband came under the sway of death. Seeing his daughter widowed, the king was filled with grief,
and the king, afflicted with sorrow, said to his wife: "Good lady, this sorrow has arisen, very hard to bear as long as we live.
She cannot be protected, proud as she is of beauty and youth; there is no means, wife, of protecting Bhanumati."
Hearing the two of them discussing it, the girl said. Bhanumati said: "I am not ashamed before you, though I burn with a burning grief.
Truly, no fault shall arise on my account, lord of men. From today, father, I shall never wear adornments;
I shall cover my limbs with coarse cloth, restrained; I shall observe all the vows, even those laid down in the Puranas;
I shall waste my body away, pleasing Janardana. This is my resolve, if you approve, father."
Hearing Bhanumati's words, the king was moved with affection; for the purpose of a pilgrimage to the holy places he gave her an ample treasury
and sent his daughter off, placing elders to protect her, and another armed man, and a brahmin as priest.
Bathing on the bank of the Ganga to meditate, lord of men, she daily honoured brahmins with sandal, garlands and ornaments.
The maidservants, servants and others able to protect her stayed on the bank of the Ganga by her father's direction.
For twelve years she remained on the bank of the Ganga; then, leaving the Ganga, the princess went to the southern quarter
with her ministers, to where the great river Reva is; she stayed six months at Omkara and at Amarakantaka.
At holy places of many kinds she went from holy place to holy place, bathing again and again, honouring brahmins, dwelling there full of devotion.
Going to the western quarter, at the confluence of the divine river, she saw a holy hermitage frequented by hosts of sages.
Seeing the assembly of sages, she bowed and said: "Tell me the greatness of this holy place and its name."
A sage said: "It is famed as Chakratirtha, where long ago the discus was given to Hari by Maheshvara, the god of gods, the trident-bearer, when pleased.
Whoever bathes at this holy place and satisfies the ancestors and gods will have a goal of no return, no doubt.
Then on the second day one should go to Shulabheda, ascetic lady; keeping vigil at night one should recite the Puranic story
and perform worship of Vishnu with flowers, lamps and food offerings; at dawn one should feed brahmins and give gifts with devotion.
On the fourth day one should go to where the eastward-flowing Sarasvati is, which came forth from Brahma for purification, lord of men.
A man who goes and bathes there should satisfy the ancestors and gods; the giver of shraddha dwells where the god, the Grandsire, is.
On the fifth day one should go to the linga called Markanda; whoever bathes there and worships the ancestors and gods with devotion,
performs shraddha duly and honours blameless brahmins, his ancestors are satisfied for twelve years, no doubt.
The place contains all gods, all holy places, unsurpassed; the place equals a crore of holy places and is the very best of a crore of lingas.
Whoever, pure and with senses controlled, bathes there for three nights, a fortnight, a month, six months or a year at any time,
has no dwelling in the mortal world; his dwelling in heaven is ever imperishable; keeping the observances he is freed from sin produced in three births.
A woman of good vows who remains without a man for twelve years is honoured in Rudra's world for imperishable time."
Hearing the sage's words she was filled with the greatest joy; then she bathed in the holy place day and night unweariedly.
Seeing the power of the holy place, the princess said: "Hear my words today, brahmins, with the priest.
I shall not leave such a place as long as I live, day or night; let these words be told by the good to my mother, father and brother:
'She remains at Shulabheda, restrained, keeping vows.'" Fasting every other day, she gradually fasted for a month.
Ever staying at Devashila, meditating on Keshava, staying day and night on the ground, the fair-faced princess was seen,
keeping her vows, restrained in diet, the lovely one named Bhanumati. When the chief brahmins had gone, a Shabara couple came.
Seeing her there, the Shabara woman said: "There is no one like her renowned in the three worlds;
she is surely a daughter of the gods come down to earth." Hearing his wife's words, the Shabara said to her:

Give her the lotuses we have gathered and eat quickly; my mind is set on worship, and I shall not eat today.
skandapuran:91:53	I have not given it up, good lady, doing wrong from sinful intent. The Shabara woman said: "Never before, master, have I eaten on such a day;
I have eaten what was left after you had eaten, for as long as I remember." Knowing his wife's resolve, he went to bathe.
Bathing with devotion wearing half his upper garment, and bowing to all the gods, he went to Devashila
and stood there, though hesitant, meditating on Janardana. The Shabara woman placed two white lotuses in the hand of the maidservant.
Seeing the flowers, the princess said to the maidservant: "Where did you get these two flowers? Tell me now.
Go quickly and find out, and bring other flowers; with this money bring lotuses."
Hearing Bhanumati's words, she went to the Shabara woman: "Give me bilva fruits and many other flowers."
The Shabara woman said: "I will give bilva fruits and especially flowers; I have no wish for payment — go and tell the princess."
The maidservant went and told her, and the princess came herself and said to the Shabara: "Give me flowers for a price."
The Shabara said: "I do not desire payment for fruits and flowers, lady; take my bilva fruits and flowers as you wish,
and worship Vasudeva, lord of the world, duly." The princess said: "I will not take your lotuses now without payment;
take this one measure of grain in return for them."
The Shabara said: "I do not think of food today, fair lady, but only of the god;
apart from the god's work, good lady, my mind turns to nothing else." The princess said: "You must not give up food; everything is founded on food.
Therefore by all means accept my food. The fortunate ascetics who dwell in the forest
all stand at my door and beg, desiring food." The Shabara said: "I made a vow of abstinence earlier; it is the truth, no doubt.
The whole world has truth as its root and is founded on truth; by truth the sun gives heat, by truth the moon shines,
by truth the winds blow, the earth is established on truth; therefore by every effort one should not break the truth."
The princess said: "A flower brought from a garden, a wild flower, a bought one, and one obtained as a gift — flowers are thus of four kinds.
Taking a wild one oneself gives the best fruit; one from a garden the middling fruit; a bought one the lowest;
and what is obtained as a gift the wise know to be fruitless." The priest said: "Take the flowers, princess, and worship Janardana."
Doing him a kindness, she performed the worship according to rule; keeping vigil at night, she heard the Puranic story.
Then the Shabara said to his wife: "Take oil for the lamp as we can get it, fair one."
Offering a lamp, then incense and worship to Janardana, he kept vigil at night meditating on Keshava.
Then at dawn he saw people eager to bathe: some at Shulabheda and some in the divine river,
some in the Sarasvati, some at Markandeya's pool, some at Chakratirtha bathing with devotion.
All those people, purified, performed shraddha carefully on Devashila, bulls among the twice-born.
Seeing them, the Shabara then offered a pinda with bilva fruits, and Bhanumati likewise offered a pinda of barley meal.
One should feed a blameless brahmin free of the fault of hypocrisy, with sacrificial food, curd, sugar, honey and ghee,
with milk-rice, cow's products and especially krishara; having fed them, the princess gave gifts according to rule:
wooden sandals and shoes, an umbrella, a bed, a cow and a bull, and many kinds of gifts of gold and gems.
Whoever gives a tawny cow at that holy place, great king, has given the earth, O king, with its mountains, woods and forests.
Uttanapada said: "The giver of sesame gains desired offspring, the giver of lamps the finest sight; the giver of land obtains heaven, and the giver of gold long life;
the giver of a house is free of disease, the giver of silver gains the finest form; the giver of clothing goes to the moon's world, the giver of a horse shares the sun's world;
the giver of a bull gains holy prosperity, and by the gift of a cow heaven; whoever gives a bed gains heaven and fearlessness;
the giver of grain gains lasting happiness, the giver of the Veda the eternal Brahman; of all gifts the gift of the Veda is pre-eminent.
A wife, a horse, land, clothing, sesame and ghee — with whatever disposition one gives a gift to a brahmin,
with that very disposition one obtains an honoured state." Seeing all the gifts that the princess gave,
the Shabara said to his wife — hear it, lord of men. The Shabara said: "The Purana has been recited, good lady, by brahmins versed in the Veda,
and I have heard all of it, auspicious and devoted to the dharma of giving. The sin earned in former births, by bathing, giving and vows —
all of it has been destroyed by mine; hear, beloved: what is given, offered or practised in austerity here all becomes imperishable."
Then those brahmins went with Bhanumati to Shulabheda; they saw the Shabara standing in the pool with his wife.
Then, going to the north-east, to the summit of Bhrigu mountain, wishing to die, he climbed up with his wife, lord of the earth.
The princess said: "Stop, stop, great being, hear my words; why do you give up your life when you are still young?
What torment, what anxiety, what sorrow or disease is it? Your child is still to be seen; tell me the reason."
The Shabara said: "I have no reason at all, no sorrow whatever; my mind turns to nothing but the essence of worldly existence.
Since human birth is gained with difficulty, fair lady, whoever attains human birth and does not practise dharma
goes to dreadful hell even for a small fault, lovely one; therefore I wish to fall at this holy place, ascetic lady."
The princess said: "There is still time for the various rites of your own dharma; having performed your natural duties, one is purified there by giving.
I will give you grain, garments and wealth; practise dharma always, meditating on Janardana."
The Shabara said: "I do not desire grain or garments, lady; the man who eats another's food eats sin."
The princess said: "Living on bulbs, roots and fruits, eating excellent food and bathing at the holy places, you will be freed from all sins;
then any man freed from sin and pure — by that very deed you will attain a good goal."
The Shabara said: "Here in the meantime I have given up my life, seeing what is good; I will not break the truth, lady — this is my settled resolve.
Be gracious, lady, and forgive me, you and your people." Binding himself carefully with his upper garment,
together with his wife he meditated on Hari and leapt; before he had fallen half the mountain's height his life was gone, lord of men.
Seeing him lying silent above the pool, lord of the earth — at that moment, in the pit of the three forms, the Shabara with his wife
mounted a divine aerial car and went to the highest goal.
Climbing the mountain peak and joining her palms, she addressed all the brahmins and spoke these words:
May my mother, father, brother and other kin all forgive me; let these words then be told to them all.
Having said this, having performed most severe austerity at Shulabheda, she gave herself up at that holy place and went to heaven.
The brahmins said: "We shall deliver the message you have spoken, lady of fair vows, to your mother and father, fair-hipped one; have no doubt of it."
Then, taking leave of the people, she stood near the mountain and tied her half upper garment tightly again and again;
then, single-minded, she gave herself up, lord of men; before she had fallen half the mountain's height she was seen by gods and asuras,
mounted a divine aerial car and went to Kailasa; then, while those people watched, she went to heaven.
On the northern bank of the Reva is a supremely lovely holy place, where the god Divakara of divine form always dwells.
As Kurukshetra is holy, excellent and granting all desires, so this holy place is holy, granting the fruit of all desires.
As gifts increase at Kurukshetra, lord of the world, so gifts increase at Pushkarini, no doubt.
Whoever gives here even a single barley-grain of gold, O king — bathing at Pushkarini is likewise held to be all that is at Sthaneshvara.
Whoever at an eclipse of the sun gives gifts according to means and rule — elephants, horses, chariots and gems, a house, cows and draught oxen,
gold or silver — to brahmins, for thirteen days it becomes thirteenfold.
One should satisfy the ancestors and gods with water mixed with sesame; there is satisfaction for twelve years at that holy place, lord of the earth.
Whoever performs shraddha there with milk-rice, honey and ghee, the shraddha under Magha and the other asterisms given to the ancestors is imperishable.
With unbroken rice, jujubes, bilva, ingudi and sesame, one obtains imperishable fruit at that holy place, no doubt.
Whoever bathes there and worships the god Divakara goes to the supreme world, saluted even by the thirty gods.
The twice-born man who recites one verse of the Rik, the Yajus or the Saman there obtains the fruit of the whole Veda.
Whoever recites the Tripushkara mantra meditating on Divakara goes to the supreme world, saluted even by the thirty gods.
Whoever gives up his life there according to rule, best of kings, goes to the supreme place where the god Divakara is.
Markandeya said: I shall tell of yet another, the excellent Adityeshvara, which removes all sorrows, son of Pritha, and destroys all obstacles.
Other holy places, delight of the Kurus, do not attain the glory of this holy place in heaven, in the mortal world or in the netherworlds.
Kurukshetra and the Ganga, Naimisha and Pushkara, Varanasi, Kedara and Prayaga, delight of kings —
all of them are not worth a sixteenth part of Ravitirtha. Hear, delight of the Kurus, what is given at Ravitirtha.
I shall tell it out of affection, though in old age no one is learned; let all the great-souled sages devoted to austerity listen.
I heard it in Rudra's presence together with Skanda and Rudra's ganas: Shambhu was asked by Parvati what the fruit of Ravitirtha is,
and Shambhu told it then before Girija; all that sung by Rudra I heard with one-pointed mind.
Brahmins struck by famine resorted to the bank of the Narmada: Uddalaka, Vasishtha, Mandavya and Gautama,
Yajnavalkya, Shandilya, Chyavana and Bhargava, Vibhandaka in his fast, the Valakhilyas and others,
Shatatapa, Shankha, Jaimini and Gobhila, Jaigishavya and Shatanika — hosts of sages assembled.
They made a pilgrimage all around the Narmada, and in its course those best of sages came to Adityesha.
It was all covered with trees — dhava, tinduka and patala, jambira, arjuna, kunda, jata, kesara and kimshuka,
punnaga, coconut, khadira and wish-granting trees — thronged with many wild beasts and crowded with lines of deer,
with bears and elephants, and adorned with leopards. All the sages entered the forest full of flowers and fruits.
At the forest's edge they saw a fair woman in red garments, with red garlands, richly adorned, anointed with red sandal,
wearing red ornaments, with the moon in her hand, terrifying; near her was seen one like a dark cloud,
of huge body and dreadful face, noose in hand, terrifying, unassailable, advanced in years, sick and tawny-eyed,
with a long tongue, a terrible mouth, sharp tusks, hard to approach. Those bulls among brahmins, best of the Kurus, looking at the old woman —
then the old woman who was near, and the old man too, O Bharata — the two of evil deeds were questioned by the brahmins devoted to Vedic study.
The two old ones said: "All you restrained ones, stay in the midst of the holy place; enter quickly, all of you, and serve the Narmada."
Hearing their words, the brahmins of praised vows went to the marshy bank of the Narmada; seeing the Reva, the best of the twice-born
bowed, and others praised her: "Victory, goddess, salutation to you!"

The sages said: "Salutation to you, served by hosts of siddhas; salutation to you, auspicious purifier of all; salutation to you, worshipped by thousands of brahmins; salutation to you, supreme one born of Rudra.

Salutation to you, purifier of all that purifies; salutation to you, excellent goddess — be gracious to us. Salutation to you of cool waters, giver of happiness, best of rivers, remover of sin, full of compassion.

Your body is beautified by the forms of many creatures and sanctified by gandharvas, yakshas and serpents; herds of great elephants, buffaloes and boars sport in your water with its great garlands of waves.
We all bow to you, boon-giver, giver of happiness, to us bound by the noose of bondage. Bound by the noose through many sins, men wander constantly in the hells
so long as they do not touch your water, touched by the rays of the moon and the sun. For those afflicted by the fear of many rebirths and surrounded by many sins,
you are the refuge, lotus-faced one, for those beset by many pairs of opposites. Rivers become pure and worthy of worship on reaching you, goddess; there is no doubt of this.
You give fearlessness to those afflicted with sorrow and are worshipped by many gods. Mortals whose bodies are sunk in the ocean of a body of excrement and urine remain in the hells
so long as they do not touch your water, its waves broken by great winds. Mlecchas, Pulindas and yatudhanas drink your holy water, goddess;
even they are released from dreadful fear — what then of brahmins afraid of fear and sin? In this dreadful age called Kali, without merit, you shine, filled with floods of the waters of time.
Goddess, by your grace the Ganga stood in heaven here, on the path of the stars. Protect us in time as you will; by your great grace we shall go to your world.
So do us this grace: we have taken shelter in you and come to you for refuge. You alone are our refuge here, as a father to a son; you are the first deity, the wondrous source.
Protect us in time from the ruin born of drought; you are the whole form of the world.
